newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn rejects Schroeder's stance on euro.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn rejects Schroeder's stance on euro.

text.p: German ministers on Monday restated their faith that Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) will happen as planned and lashed out at opposition leader Gerhard Schroeder who had cast doubts over the feasibility of the plan.
"The euro must and will come," Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told a Stuttgart conference of his Free Democrat Party, according to the prepared text of his remarks.
The mark alone can no longer compete against the yen and the dollar, and EMU is in the best interests of Germany, Kinkel said.

Schroeder, the Social Democrat (SPD) premier of Lower Saxony who last week stirred the hornets' nest by saying the euro could never be as strong as the mark, said on Monday he would not shrink from expressing his "justified doubts" about monetary union.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the economic convergence of states that hope to participate in EMU is more important than the planned schedule, and called Schroeder a "baseless opportunist".

"Someone who knows that EMU is in Germany's interest and admits as much in background briefings, but who tries to arouse popularity for himself in 1998 through such cheap bar-room talk, has disqualified himself as a politician," Waigel told the Passauer Neue Presse. union.

Well over half of Germans oppose or fear the loss of their strong currency, to be replaced by the single euro currency, and the issue could yet play a role in a general election due in October 1998, just before EMU is supposed to start.
Schroeder, who is widely tipped as a possible rival to Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said in an interview with the daily Die Welt, "I am not in principle an opponent of the euro."
"I want there to be a broad democratic discussion about one of the most important questions to be decided in the coming years."
The harsh reaction to his earlier remarks showed that German leaders are shying from debate on the euro, Schroeder said.
The varying economic strength of the nations united under the single currency will lead workers to migrate to Germany from weaker areas, he said.
Relations with non-members of monetary union will also be affected, and monetary transfers to weaker states, of which Germany already bears the largest burden, will likely increase.
Schroeder said he expected the euro to face judicial challenges in Germany, because of the questions it raises about financing for state and local governments.
He wants the SPD to set a clear position on monetary union by the time of its party congress in December. This is the year that counts in deciding the starting participants for EMU in January 1999.
His party should give "a basic yes to the common currency. But many important questions must still be clarified," Schroeder said.
Kinkel said Schroeder's scepticism was populistic politicking, and that he was isolated within his own party.
SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine said last week that monetary union was needed to promote growth, employment and stability in all member states.
